article_title: Pedagogy Is for Kids: Andragogy Is for Adults
citation: Moberg, E. (2006). Pedagogy is for Kids: Andragogy is for Adults.
title: Address adult learners' need to know why they should learn something from the beginning of the learning experience
description: The principle holds that facilitators of adult learning should "make the intellectual case for the value of learning in improving the effectiveness of the learner’s performance or the quality of their lives" from the start. The essay argues this is most important for adult learners given the voluntary nature of most adult learning and the many competing demands on adults' time, though it is also advisable for children and teens.
requirements: A facilitator who explains the value of the learning for performance or life quality at the outset of the learning experience
constraints: Most important for adult learners, especially in voluntary learning contexts with competing demands on adults' time; employers may still dictate learning in vocational settings (Day and Baskett)
target_learners: adult learners in voluntary adult education
target_learning_goals: motivation to learn; learner buy-in for required or elective adult learning
examples: The essay recommends addressing the learner's need to know from the beginning of the learning experience, drawing on Knowles' recommendation to make the intellectual case for learning's value
key_sources: Moberg, E. (2006). Pedagogy is for Kids: Andragogy is for Adults. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED507785

article_title: Headsprout® Early Reading
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2009). Headsprout® Early Reading (WWC Intervention Report). http://www.headsprout.com/
title: Adaptive computer-assisted early literacy pattern: adaptive instruction with performance criteria, cumulative review, and printable reinforcement materials
description: The program's instructional design combines several recurring features: the curriculum "provides individualized, adaptive instruction", responds "to a child's pattern of errors with tutorials and reviews to provide extra assistance", requires that "children must meet specific performance criteria in order to progress", builds in "cumulative review ... to help ensure retention", and pairs episodes with printed Readers whose "stories only contain material that children have learned up to that point". Teachers receive generated performance reports to monitor progress.
requirements: Computers must be available to children (a mobile computer lab in the study)
Teachers trained to respond to technology issues, access and decipher reports, and redirect students when necessary
constraints: Descriptive information was obtained from the program's website; further verification of accuracy was beyond the scope of the review
target_learners: prekindergarten and early elementary children learning to read
target_learning_goals: early literacy skills: phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, comprehension
examples: Children use the mouse to navigate episodes, for example helping a worm get home by identifying, from among four pairs of letters, the letters that represent a sound they learned
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2009). Headsprout® Early Reading (WWC Intervention Report). https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/211

article_title: Symphony Math
citation: Symphony Math. (2021). Symphony Math program description and evidence summary. https://www.symphonylearning.com
title: Adaptive pacing that accelerates to locate need then slows until understanding is achieved
description: The program quickly moves students through the conceptual progression to identify their area of need, then slows progress until the necessary understanding has been achieved. This two-phase pacing pattern combines rapid diagnosis with remedial slowdown, and also alerts educators when students show signs of struggle.
requirements: A conceptual progression of skills and ongoing performance monitoring to detect the area of need
target_learners: K-8 students needing individualized math practice
target_learning_goals: Identifying and remediating individual areas of need in mathematics
examples: Once the area of need has been identified, the program slows the progress until the necessary understanding has been achieved

article_title: Knowledge Sharing through Organizational Partnerships: Insights from the SEED Partnership Project
citation: Jeffrey Max, Jeff Archer. (2019). Knowledge Sharing through Organizational Partnerships: Insights from the SEED Partnership Project. Insights Brief, Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Adapt evidence-based strategies to fit the local context and needs of the adopting organization
description: The brief identifies local adaptation as a central challenge in using evidence-based strategies: "A key challenge for educators and policymakers is identifying evidence-based strategies and adapting them to fit their local context and needs." The principle directs adopting organizations to treat imported strategies as something to be fitted to local conditions rather than transferred unchanged. It motivates the partnership-based knowledge sharing the SEED project organized.

constraints: The article states this as a challenge framing, not as a tested design recommendation with supporting data

target_learning_goals: improving student outcomes through locally adapted evidence-based strategies
examples: Educational organizations partnered with national non-profits to apply lessons learned from the non-profits' implementation of evidence-based educator-preparation strategies

article_title: Multi-Armed RCTs: A Design-Based Framework
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2017). Multi-Armed RCTs: A Design-Based Framework. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov
title: Researchers conducting multi-armed RCTs should adapt estimation, multiplicity testing, and CACE methods from two-group practice
description: The report's guidance is that analysts running studies with several intervention arms should not simply reuse two-group methods: estimators "need to be modified for the multi-armed design," hypothesis tests across pairwise contrasts require multiple comparison adjustments, and CACE estimation demands attention to its complex identifying assumptions. The principle directs evaluation design and analysis choices in multi-armed education studies.
requirements: Analysts must define the pairwise contrasts of interest before selecting estimators and adjustment procedures
constraints: Guidance is framed for design-based analysis in social policy research, including education evaluations
target_learners: Education researchers and evaluation methodologists
target_learning_goals: Applying sound statistical practice when evaluating several interventions in one randomized study
examples: The report walks through pairwise-contrast estimation, multiplicity adjustment, and multi-armed CACE identification as the three analytic tasks needing adaptation

article_title: Adding Design Elements to Improve Time Series Designs: No Child Left Behind as an Example of Causal Pattern-Matching
citation: Manyee Wong, Thomas D. Cook, Peter M. Steiner. (2015). Adding Design Elements to Improve Time Series Designs: No Child Left Behind as an Example of Causal Pattern-Matching. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 8, no. 2. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Strengthen short interrupted time series evaluations by adding multiple design elements rather than relying on the basic single-group ITS structure
description: Because the basic single-group ITS depends on extrapolating the pretest functional form as a counterfactual, an assumption the authors call problematic, evaluators should add multiple design elements to the basic ITS structure. Each element limits alternative interpretations, and together the elements provide a strong causal warrant when predictions are complex and results cohere with them.
requirements: Design elements must be chosen so that the predictions they engender are complex enough that no alternative explanation fits the same pattern.
constraints: No added design element is perfect by itself; the warrant is collective and conditional.
target_learners: Education researchers and evaluators of state and national programs
target_learning_goals: Strengthening causal inference in interrupted time series program evaluations
examples: The article demonstrates the approach using No Child Left Behind as an example of evaluating a national program with a short ITS.

article_title: Educational Technology
citation: Holly M. Hart, Elaine Allensworth, Douglas L. Lauen, Robert M. Gladden. (2002). Educational Technology: Availability and Use in Chicago's Public Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Provide adequate resources and develop teachers' capacity to integrate technology as the two most important supports
description: The article recommends that creating technology-rich learning environments requires securing adequate computing hardware and human resource support, and building teachers' individual capacity through time for training, principal leadership, and a professional community. It states "The two most important are adequate resources and the development of teachers' capacity to integrate technology well." Principal leadership to provide goals and secure resources
A professional community where teachers can collaborate and learn together

article_title: The impact of test-taking disengagement on item content representation
citation: Steven Wise. (2020). The impact of test-taking disengagement on item content representation. Applied Measurement in Education, 33(2), 83-94. https://doi.org/10.1080/08957347.2020.1732386
title: Address test-taking disengagement to preserve the content representation of test scores
description: Because disengaged responses can distort the content representation of a test event, the article discusses implications for test-score validity "along with suggestions for addressing the problem." The principle is that test developers and users should act on test-taking disengagement so that the engaged responses underlying scores maintain the content representation intended by the test blueprint.
requirements: Awareness of which items or content categories elicit disengaged responses, such as rapid guessing
constraints: The available text states only that suggestions are discussed; it does not print the specific remedies.
target_learners: students taking achievement tests
target_learning_goals: valid test-score interpretation across the intended content domain
examples: The article reports two studies of rapid-guessing behavior and discusses implications for test-score validity along with suggestions for addressing the problem.

article_title: Is Moneyball the next big thing in education?
citation: James Soland. (2015). Is Moneyball the next big thing in education? Phi Delta Kappan 96(4), 64–67. https://journals.sagepub.com
title: Adapt predictive analytics to schooling rather than copying industry practice
description: The article recommends that educators apply predictive analytics in ways that respect how schooling differs from industry, because "Predictive analytics in education can offer a benefit as long as educators heed the differences" between the two settings. It works by treating analytics as a supplement to, not a replacement for, teacher knowledge of students. The article uses this principle to frame its warnings about misidentification and teacher perceptions.
requirements: Educators must recognize and act on the differences between industrial and educational use of the tools
constraints: Ignoring these differences may misidentify at-risk students and negatively influence teacher views, per the article's warning
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly those at risk of dropping out
target_learning_goals: Accurate identification of student risk and support needs
examples: The article contrasts teachers' knowledge of students with an investor's knowledge of a stock or a scout's knowledge of a pitcher

article_title: Breaking With the Past: Embracing Digital Transformation in Education
citation: Brizard, J.-C. (2023). Breaking with the past: Embracing digital transformation in education. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/176
title: Adaptive AI edtech should be deployed as a supplement to, never a replacement for, teacher-led instruction

It insists these tools "are typically supplemental and can be employed in station rotations, during specific instructional blocks of time, or at home" and augment but can never replace the skilled practice of teachers.

examples: Woot Math supplements learning for grades 3-6 and intervenes in grades 6-8; Quill's diagnostic assesses more than 300 concepts and generates a 10-week individualized plan of 10-to-15-minute activities

citation: Yanjie Zhang, Jiajun Zhu, Minyu Wu, Huamin Qu, and Sicheng Song. (2026). AdaPT: Adaptive Lesson Plan Transformer for Cross-Regional and Differentiated Instruction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17633
title: AdaPT: an LLM-powered system supporting lesson plan structuring, learning profile analysis, and one-click transformation

citation: Yanjie Zhang, Jiajun Zhu, Minyu Wu, Huamin Qu, and Sicheng Song. (2026). AdaPT: Adaptive Lesson Plan Transformer for Cross-Regional and Differentiated Instruction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17633
title: Four-component lesson plan representation schema grounded in curriculum studies and differentiated instruction
description: AdaPT decomposes lesson plans into four components: curriculum standards, learning objectives, learning profile analysis, and learning tasks. The design draws on the Encyclopedia of Curriculum Studies' four common features of instructional design models and on Tomlinson's differentiated instruction framework, operationalizing readiness via Vygotsky's zone of proximal development. The authors state they "designed a structured representation that decomposes a lesson plan into four key components." Learning tasks are refined into atomic units with task, expected answer, detailed plan, implementation method, and design intent, enabling reuse and reflection on standards alignment.
requirements: Plans must be parsed into schema-conformant components before transformation
constraints: Knowledge readiness remains initially unknown until enriched from teacher input or LMS data
target_learners: K-12 teachers
target_learning_goals: Structured, pedagogically coherent lesson plans aligned with national curriculum standards
examples: The Learning Profile Analysis dimension covers collaboration, discussion, independent learning, and preferred thinking styles (analytical, practical, creative)

article_title: AdaPT: Adaptive Lesson Plan Transformer for Cross-Regional and Differentiated Instruction
citation: Yanjie Zhang, Jiajun Zhu, Minyu Wu, Huamin Qu, and Sicheng Song. (2026). AdaPT: Adaptive Lesson Plan Transformer for Cross-Regional and Differentiated Instruction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17633
title: Multi-agent backend with LessonPlan Agent and LearningProfile Analysis Agent providing traceable transformations
description: AdaPT's backend is a multi-agent system in which each agent encapsulates distinct reasoning responsibilities. The LessonPlan Agent parses uploaded plans into schema-conformant components (using RAG over a tree-structured knowledge graph of national curriculum standards) and transforms them by recalibrating objectives and iteratively adjusting tasks. The LearningProfile Analysis Agent generates structured profiles from teacher natural-language descriptions, optionally retrieving knowledge readiness from the school's LMS via tool-calling. The authors state "The backend of AdaPT is designed as a multi-agent system (Figure 5), where each agent encapsulates distinct reasoning responsibilities aligned with the design requirements." Outputs are schema-validated JSON with references and localized reasons for traceability.
requirements: A curriculum standards knowledge graph for semantic alignment; teacher-provided context descriptions
constraints: Traceability depends on agents generating references and reasons linked to source spans in the original plan
target_learners: K-12 teachers, including those with limited ICT skills
target_learning_goals: Interpretable, editable, pedagogically grounded lesson plan adaptation
examples: Each transformed component is linked back to its source span with References and Reasons, e.g., lowered difficulty justified by weak debugging skills

article_title: AI-Assisted Social Story Intervention for Special Education: The Design of AdaptED Stories
citation: Buyankhishig Enkhjargal, Himanshi Lalwani, Hanan Salam. (2026). AI-Assisted Social Story Intervention for Special Education: The Design of AdaptED Stories. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24245
title: AdaptED Stories: practitioner-guided AI web application for authoring, personalizing, and delivering Social Stories
description: AdaptED Stories is a practitioner-facing web application for Social Story interventions with autistic children. The library is pre-loaded with 200 validated Social Stories from the SS-GEN dataset across six thematic categories. Reading sessions use child-like text-to-speech narration, and analytics aggregate comprehension and behavioral scores with AI-generated recommendations.
requirements: Practitioner review and approval of AI-drafted text and visuals before use with children
Student profile information defined by the practitioner to ground personalization
constraints: Background inconsistencies may still occur in personalized visuals
Evaluated only for usability and acceptance, not yet for child outcomes
target_learners: Autistic children in special-education contexts, including non-speaking or minimally verbal children
target_learning_goals: Understanding and preparing for everyday social situations
Target behavior change and comprehension of social narratives
examples: Phase 3 participants completed five structured tasks: creating a student profile, generating a story, personalizing a library story, conducting a reading session, and reviewing analytics and recommendations.

citation: Tripathi, P., & Kapralos, B. (2026). AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21962
title: Adaptive system optimization targets must be aligned with learning, not just performance
description: The chapter identifies as a lesson carried forward from Phase I through the AI era that "the targets that adaptive systems optimize must be aligned with learning, not just performance." Phase I demonstrated that even simple threshold-based rules improved outcomes compared to one-size-fits-all delivery, but adaptation was driven by observable performance metrics rather than understanding of the learner's underlying knowledge state. Contemporary RL systems face the same risk: they optimize whatever performance signals they are given as targets, and if those signals reflect surface behavior rather than genuine learning, the system may improve measurable outcomes without supporting real understanding.

constraints: There is no agreed methodology for specifying pedagogically valid reward functions for complex skill domains

citation: Thang Doan Viet, Anh Nguyen Hoang, Tinh Luong Son, Anh Hoang Thi Ngoc, Huyen Giang Thi Thu, Tai Le Quy. (2026). ConnectED: A Curriculum-Aligned AI System for Vietnamese Instructional Lesson Planning and Student Learning. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28647

description: ConnectED uses the ADDIE instructional design model as a unifying orchestration layer, using "ADDIE to structure instructional reasoning, decompose pedagogical goals, and control generation flow" rather than treating the LLM as a black-box generator. The Evaluation phase feeds student learning signals back into Design and Develop, closing the instructional loop.

A static tool cannot address both needs, so future TfT systems should adjust scaffolding dynamically based on the user's workflow phase, acting as a pacemaker early and a challenger or devil's advocate later.

citation: Gonzalez-Carpio, G., Serrano, J. P., & Nieto, M. (2017). Creativity in Children with Attention Déficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). Psychology, 8, 319-334. https://doi.org/10.4236/psych.2017.83019

description: The article proposes that ADHD and creativity share forms of cognitive and neurological functioning: delayed cortical maturation in prefrontal control regions, difficulty deactivating the default neural network producing a dispersed unfocused mental state, inefficient inhibition of irrelevant stimuli, and shared dopaminergic genetic markers such as the DRD4-7R gene. The article states this immaturity "favors a flexible way of thinking that is not conditioned by expectations or beliefs", so that "Uncontrolled cognition allows us to approach new solutions or creative ideas without limitations". constraints: The article presents this as a hypothesis drawn from prior literature, not as a mechanism tested in its own data

target_learning_goals: divergent thinking and creative potential

description: The editors argue that effective virtual teamwork and computer-supported collaborative learning matter doubly in the pandemic era: for learning impact and because it "offers an amelioration for the isolation that has been felt by some more keenly in recent months". They caution that a return to face-to-face settings driven by safety concerns risks recreating isolation through distancing, and name social-network-analytic methods as one way to maintain awareness of how safety measures affect learning communities socially.

constraints: The editorial frames this as a danger and a responsibility of the journal community in the emerging Post-COVID world, not a tested intervention.

citation: Meier, J., Hesse, P., Abele, S., Renkl, A., & Glogger-Frey, I. (2024). Better self-explaining backwards or forwards? Prompting self-explanation in video-based modelling examples for learning a diagnostic strategy. Instructional Science, 52, 613–638. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09651-7

description: The article's moderation results suggest that the direction of self-explanation prompts in example-based learning should be adapted to expertise: "anticipatory prompts are more beneficial for learners with more prior knowledge, whereas learners with less prior knowledge profit more from retrospective prompts." description: The article recommends that behavioral science researchers replace routine use of the conventional ANOVA F test with procedures designed for heterogeneous variances and nonnormality, and that they report measures of effect size alongside p-values. It states: "It is strongly recommended that test procedures that have been designed specifically for use in the presence of variance heterogeneity and/or nonnormality be adopted on a routine basis." It also encourages focused tests of hypotheses rather than preliminary omnibus tests, citing the omnibus F test's limitation that it "typically does not address an interesting substantive question."

graduate students in methodological courses

citation: Chernikova, O., Sommerhoff, D., Stadler, M., Holzberger, D., Nickl, M., Seidel, T., Kasneci, E., Küchemann, S., Kuhn, J., Fischer, F., & Heitzmann, N. (2025). Personalization through adaptivity or adaptability? A meta-analysis on simulation-based learning in higher education. Educational Research Review 46 (2025) 100662. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100662
title: Adaptivity–adaptability framework for personalization of simulation-based learning
description: The article organizes personalization by decision-making authority: adaptivity is "a modification made by a computer", where the system identifies learner characteristics and tailors support, whereas adaptability "pertains to systems that human actors, including the learners themselves, can adjust", e.g. via a hint button. The framework links this distinction to the Plass and Pawar (2020) adaptivity framework and Kucirkova et al.'s (2021) personalization forms, and applies it to two personalization targets: scaffolding (amount, timing, type of prompts) and task progression (order of tasks), each of which can be adaptive, adaptable, mixed, or non-personalized. Theoretical mechanisms draw on self-regulated learning and self-determination theory (positive expectations) and cognitive load theory (negative expectations).
requirements: Realizing adaptivity requires an accurate learner model, which entails data collection and interpretation within the simulation
constraints: Learner models with even 80–90% accuracy may lead to sub-optimal personalization; adaptability may increase extraneous cognitive load especially for learners with low prior knowledge
target_learners: higher education students learning complex skills
target_learning_goals: complex skills such as diagnosing, decision-making, problem solving, and planning
examples: The meta-analysis coded primary studies into four scenarios per target: adaptable, adaptive, mixed, and not personalized scaffolding or task progression

citation: Richard E. Mayer. (2024). The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09842-1
title: Adjunct theories extending CTML: social agency theory and cognitive-affective models of learning with media

The article states: "we supplemented CTML with 'social agency theory' ... which incorporates social processes during learning, and with the 'cognitive-affective theory of learning with media' ... and the 'cognitive-affective model of e-learning' ... which incorporates affective processes during learning." Social agency theory posits that learners try harder to understand a lesson when they feel the instructor is working with them; the affective models posit learners try harder when they experience positive emotion while learning.

constraints: The article notes we are now grappling with how to represent these additions to CTML

target_learning_goals: meaningful learning supported by social and affective processing

citation: Herbert W. Marsh, Jiesi Guo, Philip D. Parker, Reinhard Pekrun, Geetanjali Basarkod, Theresa Dicke, et al. (2023). Peer Victimization: an Integrative Review and Cross-National Test of a Tripartite Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09765-x

description: Because relational and verbal victimization are more strongly and negatively related to well-being and mental health than physical victimization, interventions and policies focused mainly on physical victimization miss the most harmful forms. constraints: The article notes previous intervention research has produced weak effects overall, so component-targeting alone does not guarantee effectiveness

target_learning_goals: reducing peer victimization

examples: The article recommends simultaneous evaluation of multiple parallel components of victimization and bullying and capitalizing on anti-bullying attitudes in future research and intervention design

article_title: Should we Tell Teachers That They Are (In)Correct? How Personalized Refutation Text Promotes or Hampers Conceptual Change
citation: Anna-Sophia Dersch · Ian Thacker · Alexander Eitel (2026). Should we Tell Teachers That They Are (In)Correct? How Personalized Refutation Text Promotes or Hampers Conceptual Change. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10116-9
title: Adapt personalized (refutation) interventions to individuals' prior knowledge and misconceptions
description: The article recommends tailoring refutation-based interventions to what learners actually believe, rather than addressing all readers as if they held the misconception. Personalized feedback was "contingent upon participants' answers", telling them whether their answers were in line with scientific evidence, reflected uncertainty, or were not in line with it, thereby creating an impasse experience that increases self-implication. The authors conclude: "we recommend that personalized (refutation) interventions be adapted to individuals' prior knowledge and misconceptions", because personalization benefits misconception holders but can harm those without misconceptions.

constraints: If misconceptions are not prevalent, personalized refutation text may lead to familiarity backfire: by repeatedly naming a misconception, it gains familiarity and becomes more credible than the intended refutation information

title: Select preparatory learning activities adaptively, since adaptive selection matched or beat free student choice for both low- and high-prior-knowledge students

Its findings "suggest that the adaptive strategy in the Low-Agency condition was efficient in selecting learning activities for both LPK and HPK students": Low-Agency students improved significantly, HPK students improved only under Low-Agency, and LPK students learned equally well whether the system or they themselves selected activities. This supports pairing tutored problem solving with adaptively chosen worked or erroneous examples rather than unrestricted student choice.
requirements: A measure of recent problem-solving performance with mental-effort ratings (cognitive efficiency) to drive selection, and classification of students by prior knowledge
constraints: The study's small sample (40 completers) and confound with activity-type mix mean conclusions are not solely due to agency, as the authors state
target_learners: University students in introductory database courses, both low and high prior knowledge
target_learning_goals: Database querying (SQL) conceptual, procedural and debugging knowledge
examples: SQL-Tutor presented WE or ErrEx to LPK students and ErrEx, PS, or skip to HPK students based on cognitive efficiency thresholds, before each of ten fixed problems

article_title: How Does Prior Knowledge Influence Eye Fixations and Sequences of Cognitive and Metacognitive SRL Processes during Learning with an Intelligent Tutoring System?
citation: Taub, M., & Azevedo, R. (2019). How Does Prior Knowledge Influence Eye Fixations and Sequences of Cognitive and Metacognitive SRL Processes during Learning with an Intelligent Tutoring System? Int J Artif Intell Educ (2019) 29:1-28. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-018-0165-4
title: Design adaptive intelligent tutoring systems that individualize scaffolding and feedback based on learner prior knowledge
description: The authors conclude that their multichannel findings "have implications for designing adaptive intelligent tutoring systems that provide individualized scaffolding and feedback based on individual differences, such as levels of prior knowledge". Because high and low prior knowledge students engaged in different SRL process sequences and AOI-pair fixations despite identical interfaces, an ITS should detect the learner's prior knowledge level and tailor which SRL processes it scaffolds and prompts accordingly, rather than offering uniform support to all learners.
requirements: Real-time or pre-learning assessment of prior knowledge, and trace data (log files, eye tracking) capturing SRL processes to condition scaffolding on
constraints: Grounded in learning about the human circulatory system with MetaTutor; low prior knowledge students did not engage in cognitive-strategy sequences, so scaffolding needs differ by group
target_learners: college students with varying levels of prior domain knowledge
target_learning_goals: fostering effective self-regulated learning of complex science topics
examples: Trevors et al. (2014), cited in the article, found that with prompts and feedback, low prior knowledge students took significantly more notes than high prior knowledge students.

article_title: Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops
citation: VanLehn, K. (2015). Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0056-x
title: Four knowledge-change processes for advice: reminding, persuasion, teaching, remediation
description: The third dimension names the change process the regulative loop is intended to produce. Reminding modifies retrieval cues when the student has merely forgotten to apply knowledge; persuasion assumes the student possesses the knowledge and needs convincing to use it; teaching assumes the student lacks the knowledge but knows its prerequisite concepts; remediation is needed when "the students lack pre-requisite knowledge." The Why2-Atlas physics tutor's hints assumed students knew vectors; when used with students who did not, it was less effective than human tutors who could teach the required remedial concepts.
requirements: Diagnosis of whether the student lacks the knowledge, possesses it unused, or lacks prerequisites
constraints: Remediation requires teaching prerequisite concepts; a simple statement of knowledge will not suffice in that case
target_learners: students receiving advice from tutoring or CSCL systems
target_learning_goals: applying, adopting, acquiring or rebuilding knowledge targeted by system advice
examples: Pointing hints described in Behavior of Tutoring Systems are advice intended to cause reminding; persuasive hints assume students already possess the knowledge

article_title: Backward design as a mobile application development strategy
citation: Kantorski, B., Sanford-Dolly, C. W., Commisso, D. R., & Pollock, J. A. (2019). Backward design as a mobile application development strategy. Education Tech Research Dev, 67, 711–731. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09662-7
title: Adaptive Reader technology with three selectable reading levels in CityHacks: In Search of Sleep
description: Adaptive Reader is an in-app feature that lets users choose among three reading levels while keeping scientific content constant. It "converts the reading level of the text from a story suitable for 5th grade level to either a 3rd/4th grade level or up to an 8th grade level, depending on the option chosen by the user." Text was leveled using Flesch–Kincaid (finished narrative scored 4.8), Lexile, and the New Dale–Chall vocabulary-based method, analyzed section-by-section so each section sits one tier up and one tier down from the medium text. Peers read at appropriate levels but access the same content for full participation.
requirements: Readability must be checked with both length-based tools (Flesch–Kincaid, Lexile) and a vocabulary-based tool (Dale–Chall), because Lexile has no semantic component
constraints: Simply lowering the Lexile level would not have changed true readability given the app's challenging concepts and vocabulary
target_learners: 4th and 5th grade students
children at risk of learning or behavioral disabilities
adult literacy learners
general public
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
access to identical science content across reading abilities
examples: A pop-up box at the end of selected chapters lets users continue at the same level or choose an easier or more difficult one

article_title: Assessing the impact of substituting interaction types: an empirical study of the interaction equivalency theory
citation: Hauert, S., Luo, T., & Yen, C.-J. (2026). Assessing the impact of substituting interaction types: an empirical study of the interaction equivalency theory. Education Tech Research Dev, 74, 1–27. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10563-1
title: Paired treatment materials: interactive adjunct-question lecture versus vignette peer-discussion lecture
description: The study operationalized the two interaction types with matched multimedia lectures on automobile insurance hosted on Knowmia.com with closed captions and sign-in tracking. The learner–content group viewed an interactive version with "adjunct questions with confirmatory or corrective feedback" inserted throughout; the learner–learner group viewed a non-interactive version with mandatory check-ins at the same timeline locations and engaged in discussion by responding to vignette prompts, creating their own vignette, and critiquing at least one peer's vignette. Both groups could interact with the instructor via an Ask-the-instructor thread or private message, and groups were partitioned from each other in the LMS.
requirements: Lectures required sign-in and disabled fast-forwarding to confirm attendance; check-ins were placed at the same timeline locations as the adjunct questions to keep the versions matched
constraints: The content covered explicit, declarative knowledge (automobile insurance) in a single week-long instructional episode in a paralegal studies program
target_learners: adult undergraduate community-college students in a paralegal studies program
target_learning_goals: understanding and application of automobile insurance concepts measured by a 10-item, 50-point summative assessment
examples: Figure 4 and Figure 5 show an adjunct question on liability coverage with corrective and confirmatory feedback; Figure 7 shows a sample vignette students critiqued

article_title: Adolescent user behaviors on short video application, cognitive functioning and academic performance
citation: Ziyan Xu, Xinqiao Gao, Jun Wei, Huiqin Liu, & Yu Zhang. (2022). Adolescent user behaviors on short video application, cognitive functioning and academic performance. https://www.statista.com/statistics/1095186/tiktok-us-users-age/
title: Adolescence as a developmental window of susceptibility to media effects
description: The article organizes its age-comparison findings with the account that "adolescence is often proposed as a window of susceptibility to various types of media effects and behavioral addictions". It holds that media-use impact is conditional upon differential susceptibility due to different developmental levels, with mid-adolescence a watershed in cognitive-developmental trajectories. The study uses this framework to predict and interpret why 12-13-year-olds show SVA effects on working memory and verbal ability while 15-16-year-olds largely do not.
requirements: Comparing age cohorts that differ in developmental stage, since susceptibility is hypothesized to vary with developmental level
constraints: The article notes the study is cross-sectional, so reverse directions between variables may not be ruled out and causal links cannot be drawn
target_learners: Adolescents in early adolescence (12-13 years)
Adolescents in late adolescence (15-16 years)
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation and academic delay of gratification
Working memory and verbal ability supporting academic performance
examples: The study compared 454 younger and 368 older adolescents from one Beijing middle school using two-group SEM with nested model comparison to test whether each path differed between cohorts.

description: The article recommends that educational agents not be fixed in a single role but actively adapt roles to the learner. It states this work "contributes to an important new dimension of designing educational agents — actively adapting roles based on the student's engagement and learning needs." The recommendation is grounded in the experiment showing the adaptive peer agent brought the most benefit to children's vocabulary learning and affective engagement.

emotive engagement

citation: Ipinnaiye, Olubunmi; Risquez, Angelica. (2024). Exploring adaptive learning, learner-content interaction and student performance in undergraduate economics classes. Computers & Education, 215, 105047. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105047

article_title: The Effect of Vocabulary Development Interventions on Cognitive Outcomes of Vocabulary: A Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Kansızoğlu, N. & Bekiroğlu, N. (2025). The effect of vocabulary development interventions on cognitive outcomes of vocabulary: A meta-analysis study. Journal of Pedagogical Research, 9(1), 123-148. https://doi.org/10.33902/JPR.202532083
title: Adapt vocabulary teaching to individual students' needs and learning styles rather than rejecting traditional methods outright
description: The article recommends adapting vocabulary instruction to learners rather than discarding traditional methods, stating that "adapting vocabulary teaching to the individual needs and learning styles of students may be a more effective strategy". It argues traditional methods can work for some students but may not suit all, and that teaching should be adapted to individual differences and create learning environments that increase vocabulary depth.

constraints: The article notes traditional methods can be effective for some students, so adaptation rather than wholesale replacement is recommended.

target_learning_goals: Vocabulary knowledge and vocabulary-related cognitive outcomes
examples: The article contrasts traditional practices such as using a dictionary to learn word definitions, writing sentences, and relying on teacher explanations with innovative, student-centered interventions pooled in the meta-analysis.

article_title: Comprehensive Meta-Analysis of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Psychosocial Treatments Investigated within between Group Studies
citation: Fabiano, G. A., Schatz, N. K., Aloe, A. M., Pelham, W. E., Jr., Smyth, A. C., Zhao, X., Merrill, B. M., Macphee, F., Ramos, M., Hong, N., Altszuler, A., Ward, L., Rodgers, D. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543211025092
title: Organizing framework for ADHD psychosocial treatment evidence: treatment type × rater × proximal outcome domain
description: The article organizes its meta-analytic results within a three-parameter framework: treatment type, rater of the outcome, and domain of outcome assessed. Treatments are categorized as behavioral interventions (behavioral parent training, behavioral classroom management, behavioral peer intervention, behavioral family problem-solving, general behavioral), training interventions (cognitive, organizational skills, social skills, emotion regulation), and additional interventions (combination treatments, neurofeedback/biofeedback, academic accommodations, academic modifications, self-monitoring). The article states: "Results are therefore organized first by treatment type, then by source of the measure (i.e., parent, teacher, observation, child product), and finally by domain assessed." Raters are parent, teacher, observer, or child source; outcome domains include ADHD symptoms, impairment, comorbid externalizing behavior, and parenting behaviors/effectiveness-stress.
requirements: Primary studies must supply information permitting calculation of standardized mean differences between a treatment and a comparison condition, and measures must be codable by rater and proximal outcome domain.
constraints: The framework covers between-group treatment-outcome studies of participants under 18 with ADHD (or well-described characteristic behaviors) with IQ not below 70, excluding medication-only studies and laboratory investigations; the meta-analysis focused on proximal outcomes of treatment.
target_learners: children and adolescents under 18 diagnosed with ADHD
target_learning_goals: improve ADHD symptoms, impairment, and academic/social functioning through psychosocial and educational interventions
examples: The meta-analysis reports separate subgroup analyses (Tables 2–4) for each treatment type crossed with each rater and outcome domain, e.g., behavioral classroom management effects on teacher-rated ADHD symptoms.

article_title: Effectiveness of artificial intelligence-driven simulation in dental education: a systematic review and meta-analysis of learning outcomes.
citation: Gadbail Amol Ramchandra, Gondivkar Shailesh M., Yuwanati Monal B, Sonone Archana, Dhamande Mithilesh, Panchbhai Aarti, Hande Alka H, Patil Swati, Sarode Sachin C. (2026). Effectiveness of artificial intelligence-driven simulation in dental education: a systematic review and meta-analysis of learning outcomes. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09390-6
title: Unified ADS framework: AI-enabled decision-making, adaptive or automated feedback, and simulation environments approximating clinical tasks
description: The review groups technologically distinct modalities — immersive VR-haptic systems, intelligent tutoring systems, and generative AI platforms such as chatbots and virtual patients — under a unified ADS framework based on shared characteristics: "AI-enabled or algorithm-driven decision-making", "provision of adaptive or automated feedback", and "use of simulation-based environments that approximate clinical tasks". The framework enables synthesis across emerging technologies while acknowledging that differences in fidelity, interactivity, and targeted competencies may produce variability in effectiveness. Pedagogically, the modalities are grounded respectively in experiential and procedural learning, adaptive feedback and mastery learning, and constructivist and case-based reasoning approaches.
requirements: Interventions must incorporate AI-enabled or algorithm-driven decision-making, adaptive or automated feedback, and simulation-based environments replicating clinical or educational tasks to qualify as ADS under the review's operational definition.
constraints: The modalities differ substantially in technological architecture, level of immersion, interaction design, and intended learning outcomes, and should not be considered functionally equivalent interventions.
target_learners: Undergraduate dental students
Postgraduate dental students and interns
target_learning_goals: Psychomotor clinical skills
Clinical reasoning and cognitive skills
Affective outcomes such as confidence and motivation
examples: The review's twelve included studies spanned VR-haptic simulators with machine learning, ITS platforms, and GPT-based conversational virtual patients, all classified under the unified ADS framework.

citation: Clemens Megan, Boparai Josheil Kaur, Dawe Russell, Avery Susan. (2026). Problem-based and related learning approaches in family medicine residency: a scoping review of four countries. Canadian Medical Education Journal. https://doi.org/10.36834/cmej.81284

description: The review uses a medical-education adaptation of Kirkpatrick's four-level training-outcome model to categorize the heterogeneous outcomes reported across included studies. It served to group studies by outcome type and identify gaps for future research rather than requiring studies to assess all levels.

constraints: The authors note the framework may have underrepresented process-based benefits such as enhanced teamwork and self-directed learning

target_learning_goals: evaluating medical education program outcomes across learner and patient levels
examples: The review grouped its 12 included studies by Kirkpatrick level, finding eight studies at Level 1, seven at Level 2A, eight at Level 2B, three at Level 3, and one at Level 4

article_title: Efficacy of adaptive e-learning for health professionals and students: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Fontaine G, Cossette S, Maheu-Cadotte M-A, Mailhot T, Deschênes M-F, Mathieu-Dupuis G, Côté J, Gagnon M-P, Dubé V. (2019). Efficacy of adaptive e-learning for health professionals and students: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2018-025252
title: Five-subdomain taxonomy characterising the adaptivity process of adaptive e-learning environments
description: The review proposes that the adaptivity process of an AEE be characterised by five subdomains that "emerged from the review": "(1) Adaptivity method. (2) Adaptivity goals. (3) Adaptivity timing. (4) Adaptivity factors. (5) Adaptivity types". Method distinguishes designed (expert-based, 'if THIS, then THAT') from algorithmic adaptivity; goals cover effectiveness, efficiency, behaviour change and metacognitive processes; timing distinguishes beginning-only from throughout-training adaptation; factors are the learner data used (scores, actions, response time); types follow Knutov et al (content, navigation, multimedia, presentation, tools). The review applies this taxonomy to all 21 included AEEs.
requirements: Researchers should report adaptivity methods, goals, timing, factors and types clearly, and provide details on underlying algorithms or AEE architecture to ensure replicability
constraints: The taxonomy emerged from 21 studies in health professions education, mostly diagnostic-testing topics, and the review notes reporting on adaptivity was often unclear
target_learners: health professionals
health profession students
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition
clinical skills development
clinical behaviour change
examples: In the reviewed studies, 11 AEEs employed designed adaptivity and 9 algorithmic adaptivity; content adaptivity was implemented in 20 of 21 AEEs and 17 of 21 integrated more than one adaptivity type

article_title: Systematic review of the current status of cadaveric simulation for surgical training.
citation: James, H. K., Chapman, A. W., Pattison, G. T. R., Griffin, D. R. and Fisher, J. D. (2019). Systematic review of the current status of cadaveric simulation for surgical training. The British Journal of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1002/bjs.11325

examples: The review classified its 51 included studies into level 1 (22 studies), level 2 (5), level 3 (23) and level 4 (1) syntheses

article_title: Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review.
citation: Okuyama Ayako, Martowirono Kartinie, Bijnen Bart. (2011). Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review. BMJ Quality & Safety. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3203526/
title: Adapt context-specific assessment tools to each discipline rather than copying them across working environments
description: The review observes that the described tools were mainly applied in specific situations such as the operating theatre, anaesthesia, and crisis management, with few tools developed for daily practice in other workplaces. Because "The importance of context in measuring the higher competency levels means that such tools cannot simply be copied and used in other working environments", each discipline or speciality must adapt the tools to its own requirements.
requirements: Each discipline or speciality must adapt the tools to its own requirements before use in a new working environment.
constraints: Only a few tools have been developed for the assessment of competencies in daily practice in other workplaces.
target_learners: Physicians, residents, medical students, nurses, and nursing students in hospital settings
target_learning_goals: Assessment of higher-level patient safety competencies ('shows how' and 'does') in discipline-specific working environments

Teachers trained or encouraged to implement the mastery learning approach

target_learning_goals: Cognitive learning outcome in quantitative chemistry

description: The article concludes the LAPS-Heuristic model "is effective to be used in the process of learning, especially in order to improve students' critical thinking skills," while stating that adoption demands patience and perseverance from teachers. Because students are initially unfamiliar with problem solving, the first meetings need more direction, and discussion plus presentation cycles take longer than conventional learning.

The model requires more time allocation than conventional learning

Government and university authorities should support and encourage usage of blended learning platforms

title: Adopt Blackboard-based instruction in EFL teaching methods courses because it provides equal participation, accessibility, and multiple interaction modes
description: The article recommends integrating Blackboard-based instruction into EFL teaching methods courses because its comparative effectiveness was demonstrated: it provides "learners with equal opportunities for participation", increased accessibility at anytime and anywhere, and multiple opportunities to interact with teachers, peers, course material and activities. examples: The study's experimental group received instruction via Blackboard Collaborate while studying their teaching methods course, and outperformed the traditionally taught control group on the post-test

citation: Inuwa, U., Abdullah, Z., & Hassan, H. (2018). A Mixed-Method Study of the Effect of the Demonstration Method on Students' Achievement in Financial Accounting. International Journal of Instruction, 11(4), 577-592. https://www.e-iji.net
title: Adopt the demonstration method — step-by-step explanation with examples, questions at each step, and end-of-lesson practice tasks — to improve financial accounting achievement
description: The article recommends that financial accounting teachers replace the conventional teacher-dominated approach with the demonstration method, in which "the teachers explain the lesson step -by-step to the students and show them all the procedures in the lesson". Students observe, are questioned and ask questions at each step, and then perform tasks modelled by the teacher. The recommendation rests on the study's significant post-test advantage for the demonstration group.
requirements: Teachers need orientation in the method; in the study the six selected teachers received a one-week orientation before the experiment
constraints: The article limits generalization to level two financial accounting students of secondary school and recommends further study of other levels and of knowledge retention

target_learning_goals: financial accounting achievement
examples: In the study's experimental classes, teachers explained each step with clear examples, asked and took questions at each step, had some students practise while others observed, and finally had all students perform the task

article_title: Extensions beyond Program Impacts: Conceptual and Methodological Considerations in Studying the Implementation of a Preschool Social Emotional Learning Program
citation: Choles JR, Roeser RW and Mashburn AJ (2022) Extensions beyond program impacts: Conceptual and methodological considerations in studying the implementation of a preschool social emotional learning program. Front. Educ. 7:1035730. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2022.1035730
title: Balance adherence with flexibility: require adherence to core intervention principles while allowing flexible implementation that retains each component's function
description: The article frames the adherence/adaptation tradeoff as a central design problem for FOI measurement: "researchers must balance the desire for internal validity with an understanding that achieving high-quality implementation often requires the implementation agent and intervention agents to be afforded flexibility in meeting the needs of participants and contextual demands." Following Fixsen et al. (2005), the authors recommend requiring adherence to main intervention principles while allowing flexibility in processes and strategies that retains the component's objective or function. Their adherence measures capture use of scaffolds, presence/absence of core components, and the degree the component's objective was met, with space to qualitatively describe adaptations.
requirements: Adherence measures that capture multiple dimensions (presence/absence of core components and degree objective was met) to capture nuance across classroom implementation
Qualitative space to describe adaptations moving outside the program's flexible options
constraints: Adaptations may impact implementation in a complex way, potentially increasing quality of delivery and responsiveness while simultaneously reducing adherence to the program as prescribed
target_learners: preschool teachers implementing the curriculum
preschool children in their classrooms
target_learning_goals: faithful yet flexible implementation of SEL curriculum activities and practices
examples: The MindUP manual builds in flexibility for the brain break, including multiple scaffolded implementation options and flexibility regarding location/time of day and group structure

article_title: Structuring Cooperative Learning in Teaching English Pronunciation
citation: Hsuan-Yu Chen (Jack) & Jaya S. Goswami. (2011). Structuring Cooperative Learning in Teaching English Pronunciation. English Language Teaching, 4(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v4n3p26
title: Allow adequate incubation time for cooperative learning elements before expecting measurable academic gains, especially with learners unfamiliar with the format
description: The article argues that cooperative learning elements, especially social skills, must be not only structured but "fermented" in learners before CL structures can yield measurable academic advantages. In the study, time devoted to training the CL group in the format was judged inadequate to merit a significant performance change, and the authors state adequate time for instruction and fermentation is definitely needed in future studies.
requirements: Adequate time for instruction and fermentation of cooperative learning elements
Initial training in appropriate social skills and consistent monitoring of group interactions
constraints: Short-term experiments may not capture CL effects; the study's six-week intervention was judged too short for learners unfamiliar with the CL pedagogical style
target_learners: English language learners unfamiliar with cooperative learning formats
target_learning_goals: English pronunciation skills
academic and non-academic content learned through collaboration
examples: The CL group's available phonetic/phonological instruction time was less than the CV group's because training in CL elements and implementing the structures preceded instruction

metacognition

article_title: Innovation in Early Math Education: The Whole Teacher Approach to Professional Development
citation: McCray, J. & Chen, J.-Q. (2013). Innovation in Early Math Education: The Whole Teacher Approach to Professional Development. Proceedings of the 35th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education. https://www.pmena.org/pmena-proceedings/
title: Professional development should explicitly address teachers' attitudes toward the content area
description: The article argues that teacher attitudes toward a content area or instructional practice are closely related to knowledge acquisition and classroom practice yet are rarely addressed in PD. In early mathematics, "a large portion of early childhood teachers describe themselves as math phobic," and such attitudes leave an imprint on children. By explicitly addressing early childhood teachers' attitudes toward math, PD is more likely to produce positive change in teaching.
requirements: PD must include deliberate work on attitudes and confidence, not only knowledge and skills
constraints: Grounded in early mathematics, where math anxiety among early childhood teachers is common
target_learners: Early childhood teachers with math anxiety or low confidence in math teaching
target_learning_goals: Positive teacher attitudes toward mathematics
Improved math teaching practice
examples: The ABC-EM survey of Attitudes, Beliefs, and Confidence in Early Math was used to measure attitude change in the program evaluation

article_title: Empirical Study of Formative Evaluation in Adult ESL Teaching
citation: Qin Yi. (2012). Empirical Study of Formative Evaluation in Adult ESL Teaching. English Language Teaching, 5(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n2p27
title: Adult learner characteristics framework: self-directed self-concept, practical cognitive orientation, and experience-based knowledge acquisition
description: The article organizes adult ESL learners' traits along four axes: learning style shaped by examination-oriented, non-communicative prior schooling; psychological characteristics, citing Knowles's claim that the adult self-concept moves from "a dependent personality" toward "a self-directed human being"; cognitive characteristics, citing Brown's view that adults rely on problem-solving cognitive mechanisms rather than innate acquisition; and knowledge acquisition, where accumulated life and job experience supports deduction and inference of abstract rules.
requirements: Teaching must be tailored to adults' diversified backgrounds and practical, utilitarian purposes rather than taught as for full-time traditional students
constraints: The framework is presented as background synthesis of cited authors (Knowles, Brown, Reid) rather than tested in the study itself
target_learners: adult learners in continuous-education colleges
target_learning_goals: English as a second language proficiency suited to practical and occupational purposes
examples: The article cites Gardner's distinction between instrumental motivation (passing exams, finding jobs) and integrative motivation (communicating with native speakers), holding that instrumental motivation plays the determinative role for Chinese adult learners

article_title: Assessing the Effect of Cooperative Learning on Financial Accounting Achievement among Secondary School Students

Implementation via a structured cooperative technique such as STAD

article_title: Exploration of the Factors That Support Learning: Web-Based Activity and Testing Systems in Community College Algebra
citation: Shandy Hauk, Bryan Matlen. (2017). Exploration of the Factors that Support Learning: Web-based Activity and Testing Systems in Community College Algebra. WestEd. https://www.wested.org

description: The intervention under study is a particular adaptive web-based activity and testing system assigned to half the instructors at each participating community college. citation: Amoush, K. H. (2015). The Impact of Employing Brainstorming Strategy on Improving Writing Performance of English Major Students at Balqa Applied University in Jordan. Journal of Education and Practice, 6(35). https://www.iiste.org

Creative thinking skill

English reading comprehension
examples: The researcher applied the five phases to build a computer program from Action Pack 9 modules 5 and 6, working with a computer engineer and piloting the program before classroom use

Learners at upper-intermediate to advanced proficiency preparing for IELTS

target_learning_goals: Overall IELTS exam performance across listening, reading, writing, and speaking
examples: Group 1 participants were given a mock test every session for 10 sessions over 3 months, with the four test sections administered and results emailed prior to the next session

article_title: Effect of Round-Robin Instructional Strategy on Senior Secondary School Students' Interest in Electrochemistry in Federal Capital Territory Abuja Nigeria
citation: Adigun Folaranmi A; Grace A. Ajagun; Madu Samuel (2019). title: Adopt Round-robin instructional strategy when teaching difficult chemistry concepts such as electrochemistry
description: The article recommends that chemistry teachers use the Round-robin instructional strategy, an activity-oriented, student-centred strategy, when teaching difficult concepts like electrochemistry, because its use raised students' interest more than conventional teaching in the study. article_title: Teaching Primary Grade Students Perfectionism through Cartoons Compared to Bibliotherapy
citation: Zousel, M. L., Rule, A. C., & Logan, S. R. (2013). Teaching Primary Grade Students Perfectionism through Cartoons Compared to Bibliotherapy. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 5(2), 199-218. www.iejee.com
title: Adaptive versus maladaptive perfectionism framework presented to young children as healthy versus unhealthy perfectionism
description: The article organizes perfectionism as a multidimensional construct with adaptive and maladaptive forms. "Adaptive perfectionists adhere to high standards, experiencing pleasure and satisfaction even when falling short of goals", showing organization, conscientiousness, and flexibility. Maladaptive perfectionists set unrealistic goals, feel guilt over imperfect performance, cannot feel pride, and show procrastination, anxiety, and depression. The study taught these ideas to first- through third-graders using the child-friendly terms 'healthy' and 'unhealthy' perfectionism.

constraints: The article notes positive and negative perfectionism characteristics are not mutually exclusive and have been found to be positively correlated

gifted and high-performing students
target_learning_goals: recognizing adaptive and maladaptive perfectionist traits
managing perfectionistic tendencies in psychologically healthy ways
examples: The four lessons in both conditions taught concepts such as 'Some perfectionism is good, but it can be “bad” or unhealthy also' and 'All or none thinking indicates unhealthy perfectionism'

description: The article concludes that teaching practice shapes how learners approach and view learning, and that teachers should examine their own practice. language teachers

intrinsic motivation
effective learning

Problem solving ability

article_title: The Effect of Dual N-Back Task Training on Phonological Memory Expansion in Adult EFL Learners at the Beginner Level

title: Adaptive difficulty in working-memory training: adjust task difficulty to each trainee's skill level to sustain high training demand
description: The article endorses adaptive training tasks, citing Buschkuehl and Jaeggi (2010): "a training task should be adaptive in difficulty so that the difficulty level of the training task matches the skill level of each participant, thus providing a relatively similar high level of training demand to all participants." In the study, the dual n-back n-level was raised after average scores of 80% or greater and lowered after three blocks below 50%.

examples: The experimental groups trained with Brain Workshop 4.8.4, where the n-level increased by one if the average score was 80% or greater and decreased by one after three blocks scored below 50%

article_title: A Student-Centered Guest Lecturing: A Constructivism Approach to Promote Student Engagement
citation: Lei Li; Rong Guo. (2015). A student-centered guest lecturing: A constructivism approach to promote student engagement. Journal of Instructional Pedagogies, 15. http://www.aabri.com/copyright.html
title: Adopt student-centered guest lecturing to promote engagement in online courses, provided resources and instructor workload are addressed
description: The article recommends its constructivist, student-centered guest lecturing approach for higher-education colleagues seeking increased student engagement and active learning, since the pilot "showed promising result". The article also warns the approach may significantly increase instructor workload in designing, coordinating, and executing the process.

Manpower and technology to record and produce guest lecture videos

The engagement measurement itself needs further research to be more theoretically grounded
Instructor workload may increase substantially

active learning

article_title: Using Advance Organizers to Enhance Pupils' Achievement in Learning Poetry in English Language
citation: Mary Muiruri, Patriciah Wambugu, Kuria Wamukuru. (2016). Using Advance Organizers to Enhance Pupils' Achievement in Poetry in English Language. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(31). https://www.iiste.org
title: Advance Organizers as Ausubel-derived bridging devices that link prior knowledge to new lesson content
description: Advance Organizers (AO) are introductory devices, used "at the beginning of lessons in which new information is to be learned", that "help learners to link prior knowledge to an existing cognitive structure and indicate to the learner what information from a lesson will be important". In this study the AO took graphic form — KWL charts, pictures, photographs and Venn diagrams on various poems — serving "as a bridge to help pupils link what they read and recite from the poems and the important information to be learnt". The article attributes to Joyce & Weil three purposes: directing learners to what is important, highlighting relationships among ideas, and reminding learners of prior knowledge.
requirements: Used at the start of lessons where new information is to be learned
Teachers trained in AO use (here via a teachers' induction manual)
constraints: Studied with class seven pupils learning poetry in English in a Kenyan primary context
target_learners: primary school pupils (class seven)
target_learning_goals: achievement in poetry in English language
meaningful learning by linking prior to new knowledge
examples: Graphic AO in the form of charts, Venn diagrams, pictures and photographs on various poems were used over a three-week treatment period

citation: Alireza Hamzeh. (2016). Investigating the Washback Effects of Task-based Instruction on the Iranian EFL Learners' Vocabulary Learning. English Language Teaching, 9(12). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n12p16
title: Adapt task features to foster task-based vocabulary retention
description: Based on the study's findings, the author urges teachers and curriculum designers to deliberately select and tune task characteristics when using task-based assessment for vocabulary learning. The article states "the result of this study urges teachers and task/curriculum designers to adapt task features and predict what task would best deserve academic and curriculum application in terms of fostering task-based vocabulary retention." constraints: The article frames this as a call following one small quasi-experimental study; it also notes washback research has barely addressed students' perspectives

EFL institute students

article_title: Machine Learning-Based App for Self-Evaluation of Teacher-Specific Instructional Style and Tools
citation: Fedor Duzhin and Anders Gustafsson. (2018). Machine Learning-Based App for Self-Evaluation of Teacher-Specific Instructional Style and Tools. Educ. Sci. 2018, 8, 7. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci8010007
title: Free app that computes Added Values and produces visuals for educator-run quasi-experiments
description: The article's main contribution is 'an app that allows the user to extract insights from data collected during the normal process of teaching a course'. Built on a machine-learning algorithm (symbolic regression via DataModeler on Wolfram Mathematica), it 'calculates added values and produces visuals' so that educators without advanced methodological training can control for measurable confounding factors. The app itself is free and shared with the educational community, though it requires proprietary software licenses.
requirements: Educators must buy a license for Wolfram Mathematica and a license for DataModeler, even though the app itself is free of charge
constraints: It is not meant to replace a rigorous experimental setup
It runs on proprietary software; the authors plan a free online version in the future
target_learners: university undergraduates
target_learning_goals: evaluating the efficacy of teaching methods and instructional tools from routinely collected score data
examples: The app would have let instructors in the authors' university clicker trial support their subjective feedback with hard data
Even if quasi-experiment results are undetermined, the app still calculates Added Values for interviewing high- and low-performing students

article_title: Evaluating an Adaptive Equity-Oriented Pedagogy: A Study of Its Impacts in Higher Education
citation: Phuong, A. E., Nguyen, J., & Mariea, D. (2017). Evaluating an Adaptive Equity-Oriented Pedagogy: A Study of its Impacts in Higher Education. The Journal of Effective Teaching, 17(2), 5-44. https://uncw.edu/jet
title: Adaptive equity-oriented pedagogy: a hybrid of democratic, assessment-driven, strengths-based, multimodal, and game-based instructional strategies
description: The article's central framework is an "adaptive equity -oriented pedagogy" that hybridizes specific components of democratic, assessment-driven, strengths-based, multimodal, and game-based pedagogies. Instructors collect weekly ungraded pre- and post-tests, interest surveys, and anonymous course-feedback forms, then adjust practices such as modeling skills, in-class practice, low-stakes feedback, and feedback incorporation. Multimodal instruction is described as a synthesis of "PowerPoint lectures, simulations, role -playing, dialogues, technology, music production, and art" within a universal design for learning framework, and game-based mechanics let students redo graded assignments and earn points as teams.

Students must have voice in co-constructing classroom guidelines, assessment models, and their projects
Graded assignments and assessments must be redoable, and collaborative point thresholds must be reachable for students to pass each lesson
constraints: The study oversampled historically underrepresented groups, so the samples are not representative of other higher education institutions
The treatment course was taught before the control course to mitigate instructor rehearsal effects

target_learning_goals: mastering rigorous course objectives (94% or higher)
applying course concepts through a community-organizing project
growth mindset and reduced stereotype threat
examples: Instructors provided lectures at the beginning of class for foundational knowledge, followed by dialogues and multimodal activities, after student feedback showed opening problem-posing privileged verbally confident students

article_title: Effect of Problem-Based Learning on Senior Secondary School Students' Achievements in Further Mathematics
citation: Alfred Olufemi Fatade, David Mogari, Abayomi Adelaja Arigbabu. (2013). EFFECT OF PROBLEM-BASED LEARNING ON SENIOR SECONDARY SCHOOL STUDENTS’ ACHIEVEMENTS IN FURTHER MATHEMATICS. Acta Didactica Napocensia, Volume 6, Number 3. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN/2065-1430
title: Adopt problem-based learning as an alternative instructional strategy to the traditional method in Further Mathematics classrooms and integrate its philosophy into pre-service teacher preparation

article_title: The Effects of Using Jigsaw Method Based on Cooperative Learning Model in the Undergraduate Science Laboratory Practices

experience implementing modern teaching methods during pre-service training

article_title: Interactional Feedback in Naturalistic Interaction between L2 English Learners
citation: Mahishi Ranaweera. (2015). Interactional Feedback in Naturalistic Interaction between L2 English Learners. English Language Teaching, 8(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n11p47

intensive English program students

citation: Tsikas Stefanos A.; Kieca Martin. (2026). Student background, admission routes, and academic success: a structural mediation analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09068-z
title: Anchor admissions in criteria with demonstrated predictive validity rather than compensating for background with complex non-cognitive selection tools
description: The article recommends that medical schools promote fairness by "maintaining transparent, evidence-based admission systems anchored in criteria with demonstrated predictive validity for study success" rather than compensating for background through increasingly complex non-cognitive selection tools. This follows from findings that inequalities arise before university admission and that routes emphasizing non-cognitive criteria were independently associated with lower performance. The authors also note structured instruments such as MMIs and SJTs that maintain a clear link to relevant competencies appear promising.

constraints: The authors issue a cautionary signal against overemphasizing criteria weakly linked to academic outcomes, while noting prior vocational training may still reward genuine applicant achievements

target_learning_goals: fair and valid selection for academic success in medical education
examples: At MHH, the university-specific quota combines Abitur grades, aptitude test results, and non-cognitive criteria such as prior medical or voluntary service experience

description: An observational instrument developed in the study that translates the adaptive expert framework into observable behavioural markers for cognitive ethnography. It defines markers for three constructs: epistemic distance (e.g., "Looking up information, acts of surprise or simply stating 'I do not know'"), self-regulation (e.g., "ordering more tests or seeking help"), and orientation to novel content (e.g., "Seeking learning opportunities"). The analysis then organised observations into taxonomic tables structured by actor, moderator, and consequence, integrating observations of cognitive artifacts such as patient journals and technological aids.
requirements: Researchers must specify observable behaviours demonstrating the cognitive phenomenon studied, as cognitive ethnography "requires the researcher to specify observable behaviours"
constraints: Reliability was enhanced by including more than one investigator in the analytic process; operationalisations were continually refined during data collection
target_learners: PGY-1 residents in emergency departments
target_learning_goals: Identifying adaptive practices during clinical decision-making
examples: Table 2 examples include a resident using a relative's text message to explore the problem space and a resident saving patients in the electronic patient journal to follow outcomes
