article_title: Decreasing the options' number in multiple choice questions in the assessment of senior medical students and its effect on exam psychometrics and distractors' function.
citation: Al-lawama Manar, Kumwenda Ben. (2023). Decreasing the options’ number in multiple choice questions in the assessment of senior medical students and its effect on exam psychometrics and distractors’ function. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04206-3
title: Adopt three-option MCQs after a school-specific review of item quality and distractor functioning
description: The article recommends reducing MCQs from five to three options because three-option tests matched five-option tests on reliability, difficulty and discrimination while cutting administration time and reducing non-functioning distractors. It stresses that "the goal is not simply to have fewer distractors, but fewer well-functioning distractors." Rather than a blanket switch, each medical school should audit its own exams' reliability and NFD frequency before adopting the format.
requirements: Perform an extensive review of the school's MCQ tests, calculating exam reliability and assessing the frequency of non-functioning distractors before switching formats
Construct three-option items by removing the two options expected to be least attractive, keeping distractors plausible and well-functioning
constraints: The recommendation is based on a single randomized study of final-year medical students in one 6-year MD program; the authors state the choice of format should depend on each school's assessment situation and MCQ quality
target_learners: senior (final-year) medical students
target_learning_goals: summative assessment of clinical knowledge and targeted clinical skills (diagnosis, investigation choice, treatment)
examples: Faculty reviewed 50 five-option items and agreed on the two least-attractive options to delete, forming the three-option test
The three-option test was allotted proportionally less time (60 vs 70 minutes), 8 seconds per option

article_title: Admission criteria and academic performance in medical school.
citation: Tamimi Ahmad, Hassuneh Mariam, Tamimi Iskandar, Juweid Malik, Shibli Dana, AlMasri Batool, Tamimi Faleh. (2023). Admission criteria and academic performance in medical school. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04251-y
title: Admission pathway and high school degree type as predictors of medical student academic performance
description: The article advances the framework that admission criteria — the quota pathway through which a student enters and the type of high school degree presented — predict medical school outcomes of on-time graduation and graduating GPA. The authors state the hypothesis that "admission pathway and type of high school degree considered for university admission in a Jordanian medical school could predict student academic performance in the medical school", and conclude that these criteria "can predict likelihood to graduate and graduation GPA of medical students".
requirements: A heterogeneous applicant pool holding multiple high school degree types and admitted through multiple quota pathways, enabling comparison of criteria against later performance
constraints: Tested in a single institution (University of Jordan Faculty of Medicine) with a relatively small sample; socioeconomic status was not analyzed and long-term professional performance was not analyzed
target_learners: Medical school applicants and medical students
target_learning_goals: Predicting on-time graduation and graduating GPA from admission criteria
examples: The framework was instantiated in a retrospective cohort of 808 students admitted in 2012 and 2013, spanning six quota pathways and 17 high school degree types

description: The article situates its e-module within three adult learning theories. Its didactic content is "rooted in cognitivism", its embedded case-based quizzes "pair cognitivism with experiential learning", and its unconstrained delivery aligns with self-directed learning theory, "which states that adults can plan, manage, and monitor their own education". The authors use this framing to argue the module matches the preferred, commonly utilized learning methods of current medical trainees.

Delivery without time constraints or due dates to support self-directed learning

title: Ad hoc 16-item clinical record quality checklist (score 0–32)
description: An ad hoc assessment checklist developed for the trial because no existing checklist was retrieved. "The checklist comprised 16 items divided into two parts: a formal and a content one (6 in the formal part and 10 in the content part)", each scored on a 3-point Likert scale (0–2), giving total scores from 0 to 32 with a pass score of 18. target_learning_goals: quality of clinical record writing (formal and content aspects)

title: Fill longitudinal data voids by linking complementary administrative datasets through partnerships rather than new surveys
description: Where jurisdictions lack longitudinal achievement data because surveys are costly, intrusive, and suffer attrition, the article recommends creating representative data by linking large-scale administrative databases under clear protocols and validation procedures. Successive cohorts can be continually linked if databases are cyclically re-generated, supporting "sustainable research." The authors "recommend the filling of key voids in sustainable research capacity by creating representative data through linkage protocols and data verification."
requirements: A viable deterministic linkage process when datasets lack a common personal identification number
Data-sharing partnerships between academe and public educational agencies
Clear protocols and data validation procedures with well-documented management of complex cohort structures
constraints: Fragmented data authority across agencies necessitates partnerships; in Ontario, separate health and education identifiers lacked a cross-walk, and connecting to health data awaits legislative change
target_learners: Provincial populations of public school students (kindergarten through secondary school)
target_learning_goals: Population-level analysis of student achievement trajectories to inform educators' and policymakers' program planning
examples: The EDI-EQAO merging process is partially automated and can incorporate future datapoints, continually adding new cohorts

article_title: Professionals' adaptive expertise and adaptive performance in educational and workplace settings: an overview of reviews.
citation: Pelgrim E, Hissink E, Bus L, van der Schaaf M, Nieuwenhuis L, van Tartwijk J, Kuijer-Siebelink W. (2022). Professionals' adaptive expertise and adaptive performance in educational and workplace settings: an overview of reviews. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-022-10190-y
title: A triad framework relating individual, task/training, and learning/work-environment characteristics to adaptive expertise and its visible expression in adaptive performance
description: The overview organizes characteristics related to adaptive expertise into three categories: "individual characteristics (column 1), (job) task and/or training characteristics (column 2) or characteristics of the learning or work environment (column 3)", visualized in a theoretical representation (Fig. 3). Adaptive performance as the visible expression of adaptive expertise is the core; task and environment characteristics require adaptive expertise and become visible through adaptive performance, while individual characteristics enable the individual to deal with change-demanding tasks and environments. The triad adapts Bohle Carbonell et al.'s (2014) categories, broadened to cover the HRD context.
requirements: Only characteristics for which at least one included review provides evidence of relevance (empirical or traceable theoretical reasoning) are adopted
constraints: The authors state the depicted relationships are explicitly not causal, but a representation of a theoretical construct
The article notes a gap in the literature on the relation between the individual, task and environment characteristics
target_learners: professionals in work settings
students and learners in higher and professional education
target_learning_goals: development of adaptive expertise
adaptive performance in changing task or work environments
examples: The article visualizes the framework in Fig. 3, adding the individual, the task and the environment around the core relation between adaptive expertise and adaptive performance

title: Adesante SurgeryVision VR environment with head-mounted display for temporal bone anatomy evaluation
description: A medical VR environment in which HRCT data are rendered as 3D volumes viewed in a head-mounted display (HTC Vive Pro) with hand-held controllers, created with the Adesante SurgeryVision™ software. The article states that "A head-mounted display (HTC Vive Pro, HTC, New Taipei, Taiwan) with a pair of controllers was used to visualize and manipulate the 3D models in the VR environment generated by the software". It was evaluated against PACS cross-sectional viewing in a simulated preoperative planning setting.

experienced otologic surgeons

identification of anatomical landmarks
preoperative distance measurement and surgical planning
examples: Five cadaver temporal bones with screw fiducials were evaluated in VR and in PACS by five novices and five experts, with performance time and errors recorded

title: Advise academically at-risk students toward targeted academic supports rather than optional lab enrollment
description: At institutions where lab enrollment is optional, the study's data do not suggest that labs as currently administered help students complete the class or earn a higher grade. The authors therefore recommend that faculty and staff who advise students—especially students whose prior academic performance suggests they need additional supports—"should encourage those students to seek other academic support programs like tutoring or Supplemental Instruction that are specifically designed to achieve this objective."

constraints: Applies where labs are optional and administered as in this study; labs' other learning outcomes were not tested

examples: In the UAA data, full-controls estimates showed only a 2.5-percentage-point completion difference and about one-tenth of a letter grade advantage for lab students

citation: Papasideris M, Leatherdale ST, Battista K, Hall PA. (2021). An examination of the prospective association between physical activity and academic achievement in youth at the population level. PLoS ONE 16(6): e0253142. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0253142
title: Advocate for adolescent physical activity programming on health grounds and lack of academic cost, not expected academic benefit
description: The article recommends that physical activity programming for adolescents be justified by its mental and physical health benefits and by the absence of any academic cost, rather than by promised academic gains. It states advocacy "may best be undertaken with reference to lack of net academic achievement cost, rather than presence of benefit". This follows directly from the null prospective findings.
requirements: Programming advocacy should be grounded in the demonstrated physical and mental health benefits of activity for youth.
constraints: The findings come from self-reported activity and grades in a Canadian secondary-school sample, so academic benefit claims cannot be supported from this evidence base.
target_learners: adolescents in secondary school (grades 9–12, aged 13–18)
target_learning_goals: maintaining academic achievement while participating in physical activity and sport programming
examples: The COMPASS study found no adverse academic impact of higher activity, leading the authors to state that schools can promote activity "without fear of adversely impacting academic achievement".

article_title: Implementation of p16/Ki67 dual stain cytology in a Danish routine screening laboratory: Importance of adequate training and experience.
citation: Hammer A, Gustafson LW, Christensen PN, et al. (2020). Implementation of p16/Ki67 dual stain cytology in a Danish routine screening laboratory: Importance of adequate training and experience. Cancer Med. https://doi.org/10.1002/cam4.3399
title: Dual stain implementation in routine laboratories requires substantial training and experience, and studies should accurately describe evaluator training to enable comparison across studies
description: Because dual stain interpretation is evaluator-dependent and not automated, the article concludes that "setting up proper dual stain training programs in routine screening laboratories is advisable to ensure sufficient interpretation skills among novice evaluators." It further argues that "future studies accurately describe any training and previous experience among evaluators to allow for a meaningful comparison of dual stain accuracy across studies," since most prior studies lack detailed information on training and prior cytology experience.
requirements: Documented training and prior experience of evaluators before implementation
Sufficient volume of interpreted slides to build experience
constraints: Concordance findings come from slides from older postmenopausal women, where low cellularity and atrophic epithelial cells make interpretation more challenging, possibly lowering concordance relative to a screening population; only 50 slides were analyzed
target_learners: Novice evaluators (cytotechnicians) in routine screening laboratories

examples: The Danish laboratory's novices reached the recommended ≥90% agreement only after a second training course and more than 500 reviewed slides

article_title: Impact of a web-based module on trainees' ability to interpret neonatal cranial ultrasound.
citation: Ben Fadel Nadya; McAleer Sean. (2020). Impact of a web-based module on trainees’ ability to interpret neonatal cranial ultrasound. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02400-1
title: ADDIE instructional design model combined with Kirkpatrick's four-level evaluation framework for medical WBL development
description: The article uses ADDIE (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, and Evaluation) as the framework to plan, develop and evaluate the module, chosen for its "simple step-by-step organized and thorough approach" and fit with limited resources. The authors followed a pragmatic mixed-methods paradigm and note evaluation is also the starting point of re-analysis and further design modifications.

constraints: Patient-outcome impact (Kirkpatrick Level 4) was not assessed because of multiple confounders; the evaluation relied on perceived impact beyond satisfaction
target_learners: pediatrics residents
neonatal-perinatal medicine fellows
target_learning_goals: designing and evaluating web-based medical education interventions
examples: The five ADDIE phases guided needs identification, module design with an education technology specialist, development, implementation on the CHEO intranet, and a four-step evaluation (satisfaction, knowledge, performance, behaviour change)

title: ADDIE-based infection control education program combining lecture, skills training, standardized patient simulation, and debriefing
description: The researchers developed an infection control education program using the "analysis, design, development, implementation, and evaluation (ADDIE) model". Standardized patients trained in three steps with scripts, scenario algorithms, and final practice with non-participating students
constraints: The program used only one infection control scenario
SP and PRP sessions ran at different times and places to avoid exposing participants to the program beforehand

infection control performance including hand hygiene, PPE use, and safe injections
examples: Seven teams of four students in the SP group took turns participating in and observing the 180-minute simulation; the PRP group's eight teams alternated patient, provider, and recorder roles over 120 minutes

article_title: The academic outcomes of working memory and metacognitive strategy training in children: A double-blind randomized controlled trial.

title: Use adaptive control groups that train an unrelated capacity to control expectancy and motivation in cognitive training trials

It recommends controls that "effectively train[] a capacity unrelated to working memory", and implemented adaptive visual search training (Codebreak) as such a control in children for the first time.

examples: The study developed Codebreak, an adaptive visual search task in OpenSesame where the search array grew or shrank a row or column depending on whether accuracy exceeded 87.5% or fell below 75%

article_title: Subcutaneous immunoglobulin in primary immunodeficiency - impact of training and infusion characteristics on patient-reported outcomes.
citation: Mallick R., Henderson T., Lahue B. J., Kafal A., Bassett P., Scalchunes C. (2020). Subcutaneous immunoglobulin in primary immunodeficiency – impact of training and infusion characteristics on patient-reported outcomes. BMC Immunology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7418302/
title: Adapted Wilson-Cleary conceptual framework linking SCIG training and infusion characteristics to patient-reported outcomes
description: The article adapts the Wilson-Cleary conceptual framework of a continuum of health outcomes to explicitly incorporate the impact of IgG infusion and training characteristics on training/infusion efficiency, and in turn on patient-reported treatment satisfaction, fatigue, and perceived health. In this framework, "GHP represents the culminating target outcome as an individual's integrated well-being consisting of biological, psychological, environmental, and social aspects." Immediately preceding on the continuum, treatment satisfaction and fatigue influenced perceived health, and were in turn driven by training/infusion characteristics. The framework simultaneously modeled the role of disease/treatment history and respondent demographics.
requirements: Measurement of patient-reported outcomes including treatment satisfaction, fatigue, and general health perception
Assessment of training and infusion characteristics as upstream drivers
constraints: The framework was adapted specifically for SCIG self-infusions in primary immune deficiency
target_learners: Patients with primary immunodeficiency receiving SCIG therapy
target_learning_goals: Understanding how training and infusion experiences relate to health-related quality of life
examples: The article's Figure 3 depicts the adapted continuum of health outcomes for SCIG self-infusions, showing training/infusion characteristics driving treatment satisfaction and fatigue, which in turn drive perceived health

title: Allot adequate time for group cases and individual auscultation practice, and extend session duration where curriculum permits

Faculty recruitment and administrative support if the lab is split into two distinct sessions

A large-group setting requiring only one manikin would prevent students from gaining individual hands-on practice time
target_learners: second-year preclinical medical students
target_learning_goals: cardiac auscultation skill acquisition through deliberate, hands-on practice
examples: The most significant change since the session's introduction was increasing the time from 1.5 to 2 hours, and challenging cases such as hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy were made optional in the interest of time

citation: Loprinzi Paul D., Harris Faith, McRaney Kyle, Chism Morgan, Deming Raymond, Jones Timothy, Zou Liye, Tan Miaoqing. (2019). Effects of Acute Exercise and Learning Strategy Implementation on Memory Function. Medicina. https://doi.org/10.3390/medicina55090568
title: Students should adopt the 3-R and cue-integration learning techniques, and may benefit from a brief bout of walking before studying or lectures
description: The authors draw an education-oriented recommendation from their three experiments: students should consider adopting the 3-R (read-recite-review) and cue-integration techniques because both robustly enhanced short- and long-term memory, and they may benefit from a brief walk before studying since moderate-intensity acute exercise showed a memory benefit in Experiment 3. The article states: "students should consider adopting the 3-R and cue-integration learning techniques, as they may have large practical implications in enhancing learning and memory."
requirements: The learning strategy must be applied to the memory task before recall testing, as in the experiments (3-R applied to passages; cue words generated per target word).
constraints: The exercise recommendation rests on one experiment's small effect (ƞ2 = 0.01); the authors note future work is needed on optimal timing, intensity, and duration, and no additive exercise-plus-strategy benefit was observed.
target_learners: young adult students (undergraduate and graduate, ages 18–35)
target_learning_goals: episodic memory for studied material (passages, word lists, lecture content)
examples: In the experiments, participants applied the 3-R technique to narrative passages or generated property cue words for a 50-item word list, and exercise groups walked or jogged on a treadmill for 15 min before encoding.

article_title: Efficacy of a Short Role-Play Training on Breaking Bad News in the Emergency Department.
citation: Servotte J-C, Bragard I, Szyld D, Van Ngoc P, Scholtes B, Van Cauwenberge I, Donneau A-F, Dardenne N, Goosse M, Pilote B, Guillaume M, Ghuysen A. (2019). Efficacy of a Short Role-Play Training on Breaking Bad News in the Emergency Department. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6860397/
title: Add a short simulation-based breaking bad news training to standard clinical rotations because it improves self-efficacy, the BBN process, and communication skills
description: The article concludes that "A short BBN simulation-based training can be added to standard clinical rotations", because the four-hour role-play and debriefing format significantly improved self-efficacy, SPIKES adherence, and communication skills relative to rotation alone. It positions simulation as filling a gap left by clinical practice, where opportunities to practice BBN with feedback are rare.
requirements: A few hours of protected curriculum time within the rotation
Trained facilitators and standardized scenarios per the INACSL Standards of Best Practice
constraints: Skills were assessed in simulation at Kirkpatrick level 2; transfer to real clinical settings is not guaranteed
Optimal training duration untested (four vs two or six hours)
target_learners: Medical students on ED rotations
First-year emergency medicine residents
target_learning_goals: Breaking bad news
Patient-centered communication
BBN self-efficacy
examples: Trainees completed a 156-hour ED rotation plus the four-hour BBNSBT, and were assessed before and four weeks after via simulated BBN encounters with actor-played family members

article_title: How theory and design-based research can mature PBL practice and research.
citation: Dolmans, D. H. J. M. (2019). How theory and design-based research can mature PBL practice and research. Advances in Health Sciences Education, 24(5), 879–891. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-019-09940-2
title: Adapt PBL continually to align with the four learning principles rather than sticking to one-size-fits-all implementations
description: The paper recommends that PBL practice be continually adapted and redesigned so it aligns with contextual, constructive, self-directed and collaborative learning. It argues that adaptations stimulating a deep approach to learning and fitting the four principles can be called PBL innovations, while "Violations against any one of these principles may be seen as moving a step away from the initial aims behind PBL."
requirements: Redesigns should fit the four principles—contextual, constructive, self-directed, and collaborative learning
constraints: The paper states there is no one-size-fits-all solution and no single solution works optimally under all conditions
target_learners: higher education students in PBL programs
target_learning_goals: deep approach to learning
examples: Part II of the paper offers theory-based redesigns: structured peer feedback, small study teams building concept maps, splitting large cohorts into sub-cohorts, and personalized curricula
key_sources: Dolmans, D. H. J. M. (2019). How theory and design-based research can mature PBL practice and research. Advances in Health Sciences Education, 24(5), 879–891. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-019-09940-2

article_title: Mitigating gender bias in student evaluations of teaching.
citation: Peterson David A. M., Biederman Lori A., Andersen David, Ditonto Tessa M., Roe Kevin. (2019). Mitigating gender bias in student evaluations of teaching. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0216241
title: Universities should adopt bias-mitigating language in student evaluations of teaching to reduce gender bias
description: The article recommends that institutions add language to SET solicitations that makes students aware of unconscious gender and race bias, motivates them to resist stereotypes, and directs attention to course content rather than unrelated matters such as the instructor's appearance. The authors state that "universities should adopt some form of this language to mitigate the gender biases in SET," while flagging uncertainty about large-scale applicability.
requirements: The language must cue awareness of bias, motivate suppression of its effects, and suggest alternative considerations, following the three-step design the article describes
constraints: The authors note effects "may be magnified by the unusual nature of the situation for the students" and that widespread adoption may cause students to notice the language less, lessening its effects
target_learners: undergraduate students in large introductory university courses
target_learning_goals: fair and unbiased evaluation of teaching effectiveness
examples: In four large introductory courses, students randomized to the treatment condition received a solicitation and instrument stating that women and instructors of color are systematically rated lower even when there are no actual differences in instruction
key_sources: Peterson David A. M., Biederman Lori A., Andersen David, Ditonto Tessa M., Roe Kevin. (2019). Mitigating gender bias in student evaluations of teaching. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0216241

article_title: Implementation of flipped classroom combined with problem-based learning: an approach to promote learning about hyperthyroidism in the endocrinology internship.
citation: Hu Xiaolei, Zhang Hengyan, Song Yuan, Wu Chenchen, Yang Qingqing, Shi Zhaoming, Zhang Xiaomei, Chen Weidong. (2019). Implementation of flipped classroom combined with problem-based learning: an approach to promote learning about hyperthyroidism in the endocrinology internship. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1714-8
title: Adopt the combined flipped classroom + PBL approach over traditional lecture-based teaching, accepting the workload trade-off
description: This principle captures the article's own recommendation that "The combination of the flipped classroom and PBL teaching approach could be a better option over the traditional lecture-based classroom in the teaching of hyperthyroidism during endocrinology internship, although it can increase students' workload." Instructors choosing this approach gain higher post-quiz performance and better student-rated motivation, interaction and abilities, but must plan for substantially longer student preparation time (172 ± 33 min vs 108 ± 15 min) and the possible satisfaction cost of that burden.
requirements: Students must have access to personal computers or mobile platforms to view pre-class videos and materials on their own time
constraints: The article states the combined method "can increase their workload" and that "further optimizations are required" for wide implementation
target_learners: Medical students in endocrinology or similar clinical internships
target_learning_goals: Improve quiz performance and self-perceived clinical skills such as communication, clinical thinking and teamwork
examples: The randomized trial allocated 74 students between the combined approach and traditional lectures, finding higher CG scores and ratings alongside longer preparation times

article_title: Self-perceived competence in early diagnosis of cervical cancer among recently graduated physicians from Lima, Peru.
citation: Zafra-Tanaka JH, Hurtado-Villanueva ME, Saenz-Naranjo MdP, Taype-Rondan A. (2018). Self-perceived competence in early diagnosis of cervical cancer among recently graduated physicians from Lima, Peru. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0203778
title: Ad hoc self-perceived-competence survey instrument for PAP, VIA, and VILI
description: A self-administered ad hoc questionnaire developed by the researchers covering sociodemographic characteristics and self-perceived competence for three cervical cancer screening tests. Competence was measured with three statements such as "I am adequately competent to perform PAP during SERUMS," each answered on a five-point scale from Strongly disagree to Strongly agree, with Agree or Strongly agree coded as adequately competent. Two Peruvian gynecologists reviewed the instrument and it was piloted with recently graduated physicians from outside Lima.
requirements: Review by two Peruvian gynecologists; piloting through interviews with recently graduated physicians outside the study sample; double data entry with crosschecking
constraints: Measures self-perception only, not objectively observed competence
target_learners: recently graduated physicians about to perform the Peruvian social service (SERUMS)
target_learning_goals: self-assessment of competence in cervical cancer screening procedures (PAP, VIA, VILI)
examples: Applied to 520 physicians at the VI Convención Nacional SERUMS in April 2017, yielding 432 analyzable responses
key_sources: Zafra-Tanaka JH, Hurtado-Villanueva ME, Saenz-Naranjo MdP, Taype-Rondan A. (2018). Self-perceived competence in early diagnosis of cervical cancer among recently graduated physicians from Lima, Peru. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0203778

article_title: Correlation of admissions statistics to graduate student success in medical physics.
citation: Burmeister Jay, McSpadden Erin, Rakowski Joseph, Nalichowski Adrian, Yudelev Mark, Snyder Michael. (2014). Correlation of admissions statistics to graduate student success in medical physics. Journal of Applied Clinical Medical Physics 15(1):375-385. https://doi.org/10.1120/jacmp.v15i1.4451
title: Graduate admissions should weigh an appropriate variety of factors rather than eliminating candidates on a single poor statistic
description: The article recommends that graduate admissions place emphasis on an appropriate variety of applicant factors rather than filtering out candidates on any single statistic. Because admitted-cohort ranges of undergraduate GPA and quantitative GRE are narrow, it advises that "once applicants have been initially filtered by these metrics, additional selection should be performed via the other metrics shown here to be correlated with success."
requirements: Applicants are first screened on traditional metrics such as undergraduate GPA and quantitative GRE, producing an admitted pool with narrow ranges on those measures.
constraints: The correlations come from a single institution's relatively small cohort; the authors state this makes it difficult to draw concrete conclusions about how to apply the information to admissions.
target_learners: applicants to medical physics MS and PhD graduate programs
target_learning_goals: selecting admitted students likely to succeed in graduate coursework and professional medical physics careers
examples: The program's one process change was to strongly recommend the GRE physics subject test for all applicants, where previously it was strongly recommended only for PhD applicants.

article_title: E-learning or educational leaflet: does it make a difference in oral health promotion? A clustered randomized trial.
citation: Al Bardaweel Susan, Dashash Mayssoon. (2018). E-learning or educational leaflet: does it make a difference in oral health promotion? A clustered randomized trial. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-018-0540-4
title: Story-based educational leaflet "Adnan likes the dentist" for children's oral health education
description: A colorful, attractive printed leaflet in the form of a short story named "Adnan likes the dentist", designed by a graphic designer and used as the educational tool for the Leaflet cluster. It covered "proper brushing technique and frequency", regular use of dental floss, regular dental visits, dental plaque and its implications, nutritional guidelines for minimizing caries risk, and the role of fluoride in caries control. In the trial it produced better knowledge, plaque and gingival outcomes than the E-learning program.
requirements: Content must cover brushing technique and frequency, flossing, dental visits, plaque, nutrition and fluoride, as the article's leaflet did
target_learners: schoolchildren aged 10–11 years
target_learning_goals: oral health knowledge
oral hygiene practices
gingival health
examples: Leaflets were given to children in the Leaflet cluster of the cluster-randomized trial and compared against an E-learning program conveying the same information

article_title: Implementation fidelity of a self-management course for epilepsy: method and assessment.
citation: Wojewodka G, Hurley S, Taylor SJC, Noble AJ, Ridsdale L, Goldstein LH. (2017). Implementation fidelity of a self-management course for epilepsy: method and assessment. BMC Medical Research Methodology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12874-017-0373-x
title: Two-construct model of implementation fidelity: adherence plus competence including didacticism
description: The article frames implementation fidelity — "the degree to which the treatment/programme was delivered as intended" — via two constructs: adherence, "the extent to which the core content of a programme was delivered as instructed", and competence, the quality of delivery including pacing, communication and interaction. For group formats it adds "didacticism", proxied by the proportion of facilitator speech time, measured objectively with ELAN software. The framework balances rigidity against flexibility and was operationalised into a checklist-based instrument for the SMILE(UK) course.
requirements: Audio recordings of delivered sessions, trained independent raters, and a facilitator's manual specifying core items for checklist construction
constraints: Facilitator techniques could not be assessed consistently from audio recordings; the authors note a visual approach would be needed
Assessment limited to three factual modules; discussion-based modules are harder to score for core-item delivery
target_learners: adults with poorly controlled epilepsy attending self-management courses
target_learning_goals: self-management of epilepsy
quality of life improvement
examples: The instrument was applied to three modules (Basic Knowledge, Diagnosis, Self-Control) of the SMILE(UK) course across five of 18 delivered courses
key_sources: Wojewodka G, Hurley S, Taylor SJC, Noble AJ, Ridsdale L, Goldstein LH. (2017). Implementation fidelity of a self-management course for epilepsy: method and assessment. BMC Medical Research Methodology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12874-017-0373-x

article_title: The Prevalence of Fetal Alcohol Syndrome and Its Impact on a Child's Classroom Performance: A Case Study of a Rural South African School.
citation: Lubbe Melissa, van Walbeek Corné, Vellios Nicole. (2017). The Prevalence of Fetal Alcohol Syndrome and Its Impact on a Child’s Classroom Performance: A Case Study of a Rural South African School. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph14080896
title: Adapted Behavioural Observation of Students in School (BOSS) classroom behaviour coding scheme
description: The study used the Behavioural Observation of Students in School, adapted for the foundation phase, as its classroom behaviour measure. Every 10 seconds for 15 minutes, behaviour was coded into six categories including "active engaged time (e.g., reading)" and off-task motor, verbal, and passive categories, and a first-author-designed weighting based on desirability produced a per-child behaviour score. Two 15-minute sessions per learner were conducted over six months.
requirements: Requires a trained observer conducting repeated timed observation sessions in the classroom
constraints: The article notes possible desirability bias, as learners might have improved behaviour knowing they were observed
target_learners: Foundation-phase learners (Grades 1–3)
target_learning_goals: Measuring classroom behaviour and engagement
examples: Each of the 166 learners received two 15-minute BOSS sessions conducted by the first author over six months

article_title: Paediatric cardiopulmonary resuscitation training program in Latin-America: the RIBEPCI experience.
citation: López-Herce Jesús, Matamoros Martha M., Moya Luis, Almonte Enma, Coronel Diana, Urbano Javier, Carrillo Ángel, del Castillo Jimena, Mencía Santiago, Moral Ramón, Ordoñez Flora, Sánchez Carlos, Lagos Lina, Johnson María, Mendoza Ovidio, Rodriguez Sandra. title: Adapt resuscitation courses to local characteristics rather than imposing a foreign course unchanged
description: The article recommends that each educational group modify and adapt courses to local conditions, because local groups know the needs and characteristics of their population. Unlike programs that "tried to exactly reproduce the European or American course without taking into consideration local country characteristics", this program let each country choose appropriate recommendations and adapted case etiology, environment and rescuer numbers in simulation design.
requirements: Local groups who know the needs and characteristics of the population lead the adaptation
constraints: Differences between courses depended more on the educational needs of the students than on the country
target_learners: Health professionals and general populations in low- and middle-income countries
target_learning_goals: Paediatric basic, intermediate and advanced life support skills
examples: Local case etiology, environmental factors and number of rescuers were taken into account when designing simulation; AED training was omitted from BLS because none of the countries had public access to AEDs

article_title: A randomised trial of the influence of racial stereotype bias on examiners' scores, feedback and recollections in undergraduate clinical exams.
citation: Yeates Peter, Woolf Katherine, Benbow Emyr, Davies Ben, Boohan Mairhead, Eva Kevin. (2017). A randomised trial of the influence of racial stereotype bias on examiners' scores, feedback and recollections in undergraduate clinical exams. BMC Medicine 15:179. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12916-017-0943-0
title: Efforts to address differential attainment of Asian medical students should focus on social, psychological and cultural factors affecting learning and performance rather than on examiner bias
description: Because a controlled trial found no ethnicity effect on examiners' scores, feedback or recollections, the article recommends that equality efforts target factors that disadvantage minority ethnic students' learning or performance. The authors state that "efforts to enhance equality should clarify these mechanisms and design interventions to address them", naming social networks, stereotype threat and poor relationships with seniors as candidate mechanisms. This redirects intervention design away from examiner-bias remediation alone.
requirements: Evidence identifying which social, psychological or cultural mechanisms actually reduce learning opportunities or performance for minority ethnic students
constraints: The article cautions that a single study cannot definitively exclude examiner bias in all circumstances, and some individual examiners may still exhibit bias
target_learners: Black and minority ethnic medical students and doctors in UK medical education
target_learning_goals: Equality of opportunity and attainment in medical education and assessment
examples: The article cites work showing BME students' social networks may limit access to educational opportunities, and suggests stereotype threat and poor senior relationships as mechanisms to investigate

article_title: Developing an Adapted Cardiac Rehabilitation Training for Home Care Clinicians: PATIENT PERSPECTIVES, CLINICIAN KNOWLEDGE, AND CURRICULUM OVERVIEW.
citation: Feinberg JL, Russell D, Mola A, Bowles KH, Lipman TH. (2017). Developing an Adapted Cardiac Rehabilitation Training for Home Care Clinicians. Journal of Cardiopulmonary Rehabilitation and Prevention. https://doi.org/10.1097/HCR.0000000000000228
title: Adapted cardiac rehabilitation training curriculum for home care clinicians built on AACVPR core competencies
description: A training curriculum for RNs, PTs, and OTs delivered in two 4-hour sessions led by an exercise physiologist, registered dietician, two nurse practitioners, and a program director. It covers six sections from "Background on Cardiac Rehabilitation" through "Application to Practice", including exercise physiology with the FITT equation and 2-minute walk test, nutrition, risk factor management, behavioral change and motivational interviewing, caregiver engagement, and the teach-back method. Content was adapted from the AACVPR core competencies for the home care setting.
requirements: Delivered by interprofessional content experts in outpatient CR, nutrition, and cardiovascular nursing
constraints: The article notes the restricted amount of time to conduct the training limited the information included in the curriculum
target_learners: home care registered nurses
home care physical therapists
home care occupational therapists
target_learning_goals: knowledge of cardiac rehabilitation core competencies
exercise prescription and progression for cardiac patients
nutrition and risk factor management
behavioral change and patient education strategies
examples: Two 4-hour sessions were held with both sessions reviewing the same content, and sessions were recorded and transcribed.

article_title: Improving rural and remote practitioners' knowledge of the diabetic foot: findings from an educational intervention.
citation: Schoen Deborah E., Gausia Kaniz, Glance David G., Thompson Sandra C. (2016). Improving rural and remote practitioners’ knowledge of the diabetic foot: findings from an educational intervention. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13047-016-0157-2
title: Deliver professional education informally, actively and hands-on, following adult learning principles
description: The workshops were designed around adult learning principles: that "adults learn best informally and by active participation", and that Aboriginal people "absorb knowledge better through experiential, hands-on learning". The session was therefore interactive, informal and practical, combining didactic education delivery with hands-on training. This principle shaped the delivery format for a multidisciplinary rural and remote audience.
requirements: An "interactive, informal and practical" delivery format with opportunity for hands-on practice
constraints: "no longer-term follow-up to determine if knowledge was retained", so the format's longer-term effect is unknown
target_learners: Adult healthcare professionals in rural and remote practice, including Aboriginal health workers
target_learning_goals: Diabetic foot risk assessment and stratification skills
examples: The workshop included "time for participants to practise a diabetic foot risk assessment using a risk calculator tool with clinical decision support"
key_sources: Schoen Deborah E., Gausia Kaniz, Glance David G., Thompson Sandra C. (2016). Improving rural and remote practitioners’ knowledge of the diabetic foot: findings from an educational intervention. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13047-016-0157-2

article_title: Improving Preschoolers' Arithmetic through Number Magnitude Training: The Impact of Non-Symbolic and Symbolic Training.
citation: Honoré Nastasya, Noël Marie-Pascale. (2016). Improving Preschoolers' Arithmetic through Number Magnitude Training: The Impact of Non-Symbolic and Symbolic Training. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0166685
title: Adaptive computerized magnitude training games (comparison and number line)
description: Two computerized games used in both training conditions: a comparison game in which children gave the bag containing the smallest or largest of three quantities (Arabic numbers or dot collections) to animals of increasing size, and a number-line game in which children slid a cursor to position a numerosity on a non-graduated line marked 1 and 10 or 1 and 20. Both games were adaptive, with children advancing "if the child had 85% correct answers on the last two thirds of the items of the current level", and feedback was provided after each response. Each child played each game for 15 minutes per session.
requirements: Feedback after each response and adaptive level progression to keep children motivated and appropriately challenged
constraints: In the non-symbolic version, perceptual variables (external perimeter, dot size, occupied surface) were manipulated to prevent reliance on non-numerical parameters, and a mask appeared every 2000 ms to prevent counting
target_learners: preschool children in their last year of preschool
target_learning_goals: number magnitude comparison
number-line estimation of symbolic and non-symbolic numerosities
examples: Children played the games alone on computers in ten 30-minute sessions, with the symbolic and non-symbolic versions identical except for stimulus format
key_sources: Honoré Nastasya, Noël Marie-Pascale. (2016). Improving Preschoolers' Arithmetic through Number Magnitude Training: The Impact of Non-Symbolic and Symbolic Training. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0166685

article_title: Student Buy-In to Active Learning in a College Science Course.
citation: Cavanagh A. J., Aragón O. R., Chen X., Couch B., Durham M., Bobrownicki A., Hanauer D. I., Graham M. J. (2016). Student Buy-In to Active Learning in a College Science Course. CBE—Life Sciences Education 15(4). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.16-07-0212
title: Instructors should anticipate varied student buy-in and adjust the frequency and type of active learning to target student disinterest or doubt
description: Because student response to active learning is not uniform, instructors should treat buy-in as a diagnosable and responsive factor. The article states that "instructors may target areas of student disinterest, discontent, or doubt by adjusting the frequency and type of active learning introduced in the classroom, thus maximizing the impact of these activities on student learning." Recognizing the likelihood of variation in student response is described as an important first step in benefiting all learners.
requirements: Instructors need a way to recognize variation in student response before adjusting activities
constraints: The supporting evidence comes from one cross-sectional study in a single course; no causal test of adjusting activities was performed
target_learners: undergraduate STEM students
target_learning_goals: student engagement in active-learning activities
examples: In the studied course, students on average reported completing approximately six activities (M = 6.27, SD = 3.26) because they believed they contributed positively to learning, showing wide variation in endorsement across the 16 activities
key_sources: Cavanagh A. J., Aragón O. R., Chen X., Couch B., Durham M., Bobrownicki A., Hanauer D. I., Graham M. J. (2016). Student Buy-In to Active Learning in a College Science Course. CBE—Life Sciences Education 15(4). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.16-07-0212
